title: ROBIS: A new tool to assess risk of bias in systematic reviews was developed

extracted.subtask_short: Judging whether review conclusions match its own evidence
extracted.subtask_description: Assesses risk of bias in a systematic review across four process domains (eligibility, selection, data collection, synthesis), then explicitly judges whether the review's stated interpretation/conclusions are supported by the evidence it synthesized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 1 relevance rating (PICO alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: The assessor defines the question they actually care about using PICO (or an equivalent framework) and rates how well the systematic review's own question aligns with it ('yes'/'partial'/'no').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phase can be skipped when a review is being assessed on its own terms rather than against an external question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain 1: study eligibility criteria prespecified and consistently applied
rubrics_metrics.description: Were the review's inclusion criteria prespecified, clear, and appropriate to the review question? Criteria should be explicitly defined before study selection began (ideally documented in a protocol/registration predating the review) and applied consistently across candidate studies rather than adjusted post hoc to fit a desired conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain 2: comprehensive, unbiased identification and selection of studies
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensitive searches across appropriate databases and both published and unpublished sources; supplementary search methods such as reference-list checking, citation searching, and hand-searching; a search strategy combining free-text terms and controlled vocabulary/subject indexing; independent screening by at least two reviewers at both the title/abstract and full-text stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain 3: unbiased data collection and study appraisal
rubrics_metrics.description: A planned, structured data-collection form piloted before use; comprehensive collection of numerical, statistical, and study-characteristic data (not just outcomes favorable to a hypothesis); duplicate data extraction, or rigorous single extraction with independent verification; risk-of-bias assessment of primary studies using validated tools or clearly stated criteria; at least two reviewers independently assessing (or verifying) study validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain 4: appropriate synthesis method honestly reflecting the evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Whether the analytic approach is appropriate for the research question posed; whether between-study variation (heterogeneity) is taken into account; whether biases in the primary studies are taken into account; whether the information from the primary studies being synthesized is complete.' Critical aspects: choosing an appropriate synthesis method (quantitative meta-analysis vs. narrative synthesis), accounting for study-level bias when interpreting pooled results, addressing publication/reporting bias, avoiding computational errors in meta-analytic calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 3: whether stated conclusions are actually supported by the synthesized evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Signalling questions evaluate whether the review's interpretation addressed all concerns identified in Phase 2's four domains, whether the review's stated conclusions are actually supported by the evidence that was synthesized, and the overall quality of the interpretation despite whatever limitations were identified. The overall judgment is 'low,' 'high,' or 'unclear' risk of bias.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak underlying evidence vs overclaimed conclusion are distinct failures
rubrics_metrics.description: A systematic review can be judged low risk of bias even if its included primary studies are individually high risk of bias - provided the review explicitly identified, assessed, and accounted for that risk when drawing its conclusions. ROBIS distinguishes 'the underlying evidence is weak' from 'the review claims more than the evidence supports': a review can honestly caveat weak evidence and still pass; a review can also draw an overclaimed conclusion from strong-looking evidence and fail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The claim-evidence match being tested is specifically whether the stated conclusion's confidence level tracks the actual limitations of the review process and the underlying evidence, not whether the evidence itself is flawless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequential domain dependency (early flaws propagate to later ones)
rubrics_metrics.description: The four Phase-2 domains are meant to be considered sequentially - problems identified early (e.g., a biased eligibility criterion) can propagate into and compound concerns found later (e.g., in synthesis) - rather than as four independent, siloed checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing methodological detail itself counts as evidence of unassessed bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting quality of the review under assessment directly affects how feasible ROBIS is to apply; many 'no information' answers to signalling questions should push a domain toward 'unclear' or 'high' rather than being ignored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cochrane reviews typically provide sufficient methodological detail; many non-Cochrane reviews do not.
